g.text: Deliverability is not something you configure. It is something you ACCUMULATE.
Standing up an SMTP server is an afternoon's work. Getting its mail into an inbox takes weeks to months, and no amount of correct code shortens it.
The same message, two sending IPs
one message
identical bytes
a BRAND-NEW IP
no history, no authentication
SPAM FOLDER
a WARMED, AUTHENTICATED IP
SPF + DKIM + DMARC, weeks of history
INBOX
Not because of anything in the
message. The receiving provider
has simply never seen that IP
before, has no reason to trust
it, and knows that spammers
cycle through fresh IPs
constantly.
THE DEFAULT POSTURE TOWARD AN UNKNOWN SENDER IS SUSPICION,
because that is the only posture that works.
Which inverts the usual relationship between engineering and
reputation - and has one direct architectural consequence:
outbound capacity CANNOT AUTOSCALE, because new sending IPs
need weeks of warm-up. In an otherwise fully elastic system,
outbound send capacity is a weeks-ahead provisioning decision.
Three DNS mechanisms that STACK - each one fixes a gap in the previous
SPF authorizes SERVERS
example.com. TXT "v=spf1 ip4:198.51.100.0/24
include:_spf.provider.com -all"
A DNS record listing authorized sending IPs; the
receiver checks the connecting IP against it, and
-all means 'reject anything not listed'.
the gap: SPF BREAKS ON FORWARDING
If Alice forwards a message to Bob, Bob's server sees
ALICE's server connecting while the message claims to
be from the original domain - so SPF fails on a
perfectly legitimate message. Not an edge case:
automatic forwarding is extremely common.
DKIM authorizes MESSAGES
selector._domainkey.example.com. TXT
"v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIGfMA0GCSq..."
The sender signs selected headers and the body with a
private key; the receiver fetches the public key from DNS
and verifies. So the message carries proof of origin
INDEPENDENT of which server delivered it - which is exactly
what fixes forwarding, and exactly why DKIM exists: SPF's
IP-based model could not survive how mail actually moves.
the gap: it says nothing about POLICY
DKIM proves a signature is valid, but a receiver
seeing an UNSIGNED message has no way to know whether
that domain signs its mail at all.
DMARC sets POLICY and demands ALIGNMENT
_dmarc.example.com. TXT "v=DMARC1;
p=reject; rua=mailto:...; pct=100"
Two things neither of the others can do. It states a
POLICY - none (monitor), quarantine (spam folder) or
reject (refuse outright) - for messages failing SPF
AND DKIM, closing DKIM's gap. And it requires
ALIGNMENT: the domain in the visible From: header
must match the domain SPF or DKIM authenticated.
alignment is what actually stops spoofing
Without it, a spammer could pass SPF for spammer.com
while displaying From: paypal.com. This is the part
most explanations skip.
The stack, as a chain: SPF authorizes SERVERS. DKIM authorizes MESSAGES, surviving forwarding. DMARC sets POLICY and demands
the authenticated domain match the one users actually see. Without all three you are spoofable; with all three plus p=reject,
nobody can send mail that appears to come from your domain - which protects your users AND your reputation, since spoofed
phishing damages the domain's standing even though you never sent it.
DMARC's aggregate reports (rua=) are what make rolling out p=reject safe: receivers send daily summaries of what passed and
failed, so you start at p=none, read reports until every legitimate sending path is authenticated, then tighten.
IP warm-up is not optional - and it is per RECEIVING PROVIDER
week 1
~50 / day per provider
week 2
week 3
week 4
week 6-8
full volume
Send 10 million messages from a fresh IP on day one and most will be rejected or spam-foldered - and the resulting complaint
and bounce rates DAMAGE THE IP'S REPUTATION, making the problem self-reinforcing. So volume is ramped gradually, letting each
provider observe good behaviour at each level. Roughly 2 to 6 weeks per IP, and Gmail, Outlook and Yahoo each maintain
independent reputation and must each observe the ramp separately.
Three architectural consequences:
new sending capacity has WEEKS of lead time - you cannot
add outbound throughput in response to demand
losing an IP is EXPENSIVE - a blocklisted IP takes weeks to
replace, so protecting reputation is protecting capacity
the IP pool is a MANAGED RESOURCE with per-IP, per-provider
volume budgets - which is why the reputation / IP pool
manager is a first-class component and not a config file
Never send different classes of mail from the same IPs - the most commonly botched decision here
TRANSACTIONAL IPs
password resets, receipts, 2FA codes, security alerts
low complaint rate, high engagement - MUST arrive
BULK / MARKETING IPs
newsletters, promotions, digests
higher complaint rate, lower engagement - can be delayed
FORWARDING IPs
mail forwarded on a user's behalf
content you did not author and cannot vet, so its complaint rate is outside your control
Reputation is PER-IP, and marketing mail always attracts more complaints than transactional mail. Share the IPs and the
marketing complaints degrade the reputation delivering your password resets - so a promotional campaign somebody marks as
spam makes 2FA codes land in spam folders. A catastrophic coupling between a low-stakes system and a critical one, caused
entirely by an IP-assignment decision. Separation means a bad campaign damages only the bulk pool - and it hands the load
shedder its ordering for free, since bulk can be delayed behind transactional under overload.
Without a feedback loop you cannot tell 'delivered to the inbox' from 'delivered to spam'
The provider's spam decision is INVISIBLE otherwise: a message accepted with 250 OK and then filed in spam looks like a
successful delivery from your side. So an FBL feed is not a monitoring nicety - it is the input to an automated response, and
the threshold everyone works to is a complaint rate below ~0.1%, one per thousand delivered. Above that, providers throttle
or block.
complaint rate rising on an IP -> reduce its volume, investigate the campaign
a single account generating complaints -> suspend it immediately
hard bounces (5xx: no such user) -> remove the address PERMANENTLY, from all lists
That last rule matters more than it looks. Repeatedly sending to addresses that
do not exist is one of the strongest spam signals there is, because legitimate
senders maintain their lists and spammers work from purchased ones. So bounce
handling is not cleanup - it is reputation management, and a system that
ignores hard bounces will be classified as a spammer on the strength of that
alone.
You are also a receiver, and your inbound behaviour affects your standing
reject EARLY and CHEAPLY:
connection level: IP blocklisted? no reverse DNS? rate-limited? -> 5xx, before DATA
envelope level: recipient does not exist? SPF hard fail? -> 5xx, before DATA
then accept, and score asynchronously
Rejecting before accepting the body is what makes spam cheap to refuse: at spam
volumes, transferring 50 KB before deciding would mean most of your inbound
bandwidth is spent on mail you discard.
And the reciprocal rule: use 4xx for TEMPORARY problems and 5xx for PERMANENT
ones, honestly. A receiver that returns 5xx for a transient issue makes
legitimate mail bounce permanently; one that returns 4xx for a permanent
problem makes senders retry for days against a nonexistent address. Both damage
your standing as a receiver, and both are trivially avoidable by getting the
code right.
What this module actually changes in the architecture
deliverability requirement
architectural consequence
IP warm-up takes weeks
outbound capacity CANNOT AUTOSCALE - it is a weeks-ahead provisioning decision
reputation is per-IP
an IP pool manager as a first-class component, with per-IP, per-provider volume budgets
mail classes must not share IPs
outbound routing is a CLASSIFICATION decision - and it gives the shedding order for free
DKIM signing is mandatory
signing happens in the outbound worker, with key management and selector rotation
complaint rate under 0.1%
FBL ingestion, plus automated throttling and account suspension
hard bounces must be honoured
a suppression list consulted before every send, and never bypassed
a compromised account is a spam cannon
PER-ACCOUNT outbound rate limiting, on the synchronous send path
The last row deserves the emphasis: the fastest way to destroy a mail system's reputation is one compromised account sending a
million messages before anyone notices. So per-account send limits are a REPUTATION CONTROL, not an abuse-prevention nicety -
and they belong on the synchronous send path, where they can actually stop it.
